The word peeps is an informal, casual way of saying "people" — but it carries a warmer, more personal feeling than just "people." When someone says "my peeps," they usually mean the people they are close to: their friends, their crew, their community, or anyone they feel a sense of belonging with.

Think of it this way: if you said "I'm going out with my people," it sounds a bit formal. But if you said "I'm going out with my peeps," it sounds friendly, relaxed, and affectionate. That warmth is baked into the word.

Examples:

  • "I can't wait to see my peeps this weekend." → I can't wait to see my friends/close ones.
  • "I'll ask my peeps if they want to come along." → I'll ask the people in my group.
  • "Shout out to all my peeps who supported me!" → A warm acknowledgment to all my people/supporters.
  • "Where are your peeps from?" → Where are the people you hang out with from? (or sometimes: where is your family from?)
The Feel of the Word: Who Uses It and When

Peeps is a slang word. It lives in informal, everyday conversation — in texts, social media, casual speech, and among friends. You would not use it in a formal letter, a job interview, or an academic paper. Its tone is friendly, laid-back, and sometimes affectionate.

It is especially common in American English, though people around the English-speaking world understand and use it. It spread largely through pop culture — music, social media, and films.

You can use peeps to refer to:

  • Your close friends ("Me and my peeps are heading out.")
  • A group of people you identify with ("All my book-lover peeps will understand this.")
  • People in general, in a casual, lighthearted way ("Hey peeps, big announcement coming soon!" — often used to address a group, almost like saying "Hey everyone!")

That last use — addressing a group directly with "Hey peeps!" — is very common online, especially on social media and YouTube, as a friendly, breezy way to greet an audience.

While peeps often just means people, there is a subtle but meaningful difference in feel:

  • "People" is neutral and wide. It can mean anyone.
  • "Peeps" often implies your people — people you know, like, or belong with. It has a tribal, in-group warmth to it.

So when someone says "my peeps," they are almost always talking about people they care about or feel connected to — not random strangers.
A Second Meaning: The Easter Candy

In American English, Peeps (usually capitalized) is also a brand name for a popular marshmallow candy sold especially around Easter. These are soft, sugar-coated marshmallows shaped like baby chicks, bunnies, and other animals, made in bright colors. They are a well-known cultural fixture in the United States during the spring holiday season.

Example:

  • "My kids eat so many Peeps every Easter."
  • "The store shelves are full of Peeps right now."

If you hear Peeps in an American context around Easter, there is a good chance this is what someone means. Outside of that seasonal context, it almost always refers to the slang meaning.
A Third (Less Common) Meaning: Plural of "Peep" (a Brief Look)

In some varieties of English — particularly British English — a peep (singular) can mean a quick, sneaky, or brief look at something. The plural, peeps, would then mean multiple such glances.

Example:

  • "The children kept sneaking peeps through the window." → They kept stealing quick glances through the window.

This meaning is less dominant than the slang sense today, and you are more likely to encounter the singular peep in this sense than the plural. But it is worth knowing.

A peep can also refer to a soft, tiny sound — the kind a baby chick or a small bird makes. In the plural, peeps would mean several of those small sounds.

Example:

  • "Not a peep out of anyone!" → Complete silence (this is a very common idiom).
  • "The nest was full of soft peeps." → Small chirping sounds from baby birds.

This meaning is mostly used in the singular ("not a peep"), and when you hear peeps in everyday conversation, this is rarely what someone means.
Quick Summary of All Noun Meanings

Meaning 1 (Most Common): Slang for "people," especially your close friends, crew, or community. Warm, casual, informal. Used widely in everyday speech and online.

Meaning 2: A well-known brand of Easter marshmallow candies in America. Capitalized as Peeps.

Meaning 3: Plural of a brief, sneaky look or glance. More common in British English.

Meaning 4: Plural of a soft, small sound (like a baby bird's chirp). Mostly found in idiomatic expressions like "not a peep."

If you encounter peeps in a conversation or in something you are reading, context will almost always make the meaning obvious — and nine times out of ten, it will be the first meaning: a friendly, informal way of saying "people," especially one's own people.
